analysis.one_liner: Makes most of Washington, D.C. a full state with two senators and a voting representative.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached the Senate floor: after one committee hearing in June 2021, it sat in committee for the rest of the Congress and received no vote, leaving D.C.'s roughly 700,000 residents without voting representation in Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The Washington, D.C. Admission Act would turn most of the District of Columbia — home to about 700,000 Americans who currently pay federal taxes but have no voting member of Congress — into the 51st state, called Washington, Douglass Commonwealth. Residents would elect two senators and one voting House member. The White House, Capitol, Supreme Court, and nearby federal office buildings would stay under federal control as a much-reduced federal enclave, and the bill sets up a transition for courts, prosecutors, and retirement obligations. Introduced by Senator Tom Carper with 45 cosponsors — every Senate Democrat but a handful plus one independent — it got a single committee hearing in June 2021 and never received a vote in the Senate or the House.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the roughly 700,000 residents of the District of Columbia — the majority of whom are Black and brown residents of a majority-Democratic city — would gain full voting representation in Congress for the first time: two senators and one voting House member. They would also gain full control over their own local laws, which Congress can currently overturn, and their local budget would no longer need congressional approval. The state government would take over local courts, prosecutions, and other functions currently run by federal appointees whom D.C. residents do not elect.

how_it_helps.text: Admits the new state on equal footing, entitling its residents to two senators and one voting representative — rights and privileges identical to those of other states' members of Congress.
Transfers legislative power over the territory from Congress to the state, so residents' own elected government makes their laws instead of Congress, which currently can override any D.C. law.

Continues federal funding and services through a managed transition — retirement benefits, public defender service, prosecutions, courts, Medicaid rates, college tuition assistance — until the state certifies it can take over, so residents do not lose services on day one.
Lets the small remaining federal enclave's residents vote absentee in the states where they last lived, rather than losing the vote entirely.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the main costs would fall on the Senate's existing balance: two new senators and one representative, almost certainly Democrats, shifting national lawmaking. Some federal responsibilities would shift to the new state, and opponents argued a constitutional amendment should be required. The small remaining federal enclave's residents would vote absentee in their former home states rather than locally.

drawbacks.text: Critics argue that reducing the District to a small federal enclave and admitting the rest as a state cannot be done by ordinary legislation, and that the Constitution requires a constitutional amendment to change the seat of government this way. The bill itself concedes the legal risk with a nonseverability clause: if the admission provision is struck down in court, the entire act falls.

The state would control its own criminal laws and courts, including over the federal enclave's perimeter; the bill preserves federal prosecution functions only until the state certifies it has appointed its own attorneys, and bars Capitol Police, Park Police, and Secret Service from enforcing state law except as the state allows.

The state could not tax federal property except as Congress permits, leaving a large tax-exempt presence in a small state, and many federal responsibilities — courts, prosecutions, retirement obligations, pretrial services — continue at federal expense only until the state certifies it is prepared to take them over, a potentially expensive handoff.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 700,000 D.C. residents, the benefits are concrete: full voting representation in Congress and control of their own local affairs, including locally funded programs. The costs are debatable. Opponents argue two Senate seats from a 68-square-mile jurisdiction distort the Senate's design and that some version of statehood may need a constitutional amendment rather than a statute — a point the bill's nonseverability clause implicitly concedes by voiding the whole act if admission is struck down. The bill's carve-out of federal buildings addresses the constitutional seat-of-government requirement, but does not address the argument that ordinary legislation cannot make a state. D.C.'s overwhelmingly Democratic voting pattern makes the partisan stakes obvious and fuels the opposition. On the merits of representation, the bill directly remedies a real disenfranchisement — a majority-Black city for much of its history pays federal taxes and sends soldiers to war without a vote in Congress — and the transition provisions are unusually careful.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee held one hearing, never voted the bill out, and the Senate never took it up, so it expired at the end of the two-year Congress.

narrative.text: Introduced January 26, 2021, the bill was read twice and referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the same day — the standard first step.
Forty-five senators signed on as cosponsors — all but a few Senate Democrats plus independent Bernie Sanders — yet no committee vote or floor action followed the June 22, 2021 hearing.
The action history ends there: no markup, no committee report, no floor vote through January 3, 2023, when the 117th Congress ended.

Because a filibuster requires 60 votes to move most bills to a final vote, a bill with about 47 supporters and 50 Republican senators opposed could not reach the floor without unwinding the filibuster, which Senate leadership did not do for this bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The 50 Republican senators and the Senate status quo: D.C. remains without voting representation, and no two new Democratic Senate seats were created. House-passed statehood legislation also went nowhere in the Senate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Senate status quo and its 50 GOP senators

for.name: Tom Carper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as sponsor; it was his bill that the committee never reported out.

for.name: 44 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Chuck Schumer, Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren, and Raphael Warnock — a near-unanimous Senate Democratic caucus.

for.name: President Joe Biden
for.what_they_did: Publicly endorsed D.C. statehood and included it in his budget proposals, but did not make it a must-pass priority.

for.name: D.C. government and advocates
for.role: D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser, Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton, and the '51 for 51' campaign
for.what_they_did: Ran a sustained public campaign for statehood, including a'51 for 51' push calling on the Senate to waive the filibuster for the bill.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, leaving it with only the 45 Democratic and independent supporters — short of the 60 votes needed to end a filibuster — and the bill never reached the floor.

against.name: Gary Peters
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee held a hearing but never voted the bill out or reported it to the floor.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership under the filibuster rule
against.role: Minority Leader Mitch McConnell and Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Senate rules require 60 votes to end debate on most bills; with Republicans uniformly opposed, the bill could not reach a floor vote, and the majority did not change the rule to allow it.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or the independent Bernie Sanders — 44 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents — while not a single Senate Republican signed on, making this a fully partisan split in the Senate.

industries.industry: D.C. residents (as a class of disenfranchised taxpayers)
industries.note: Not an industry, but the concentrated interest this bill most affects: roughly 700,000 people who pay federal taxes, serve on juries, and fight in wars while holding no vote in Congress. Statehood converts them from a disenfranchised class into full participants; the bill's failure keeps them there.

Officeholders keep an insulated federal enclave around the Capitol, White House, and Supreme Court, with a dedicated Capital National Guard and continued federal control of courts and prosecutions there — but lose the power to legislate for the rest of D.C. and to shape its politics through the appropriations and review process.

The city's government, courts, universities, and nonprofits gain a state framework and continued federal funding during the transition, but must eventually absorb responsibilities — prosecutors, courts, pretrial services, retirement obligations — currently paid for by the federal government.
